title: Desert Survival: Josh and Chuck Save Your Tookus
summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about podcast burnout, Keanu Reeves, Ben Sinclair, and the movie Point Break, then turn to desert survival, based on Chuck's HowStuffWorks article. Topics include water rationing and dehydration, using fire, signaling rescuers (mirrors, hoods, SOS, honking), staying in shade off the ground, foot and clothing care, walking pace in groups, heat cramps, heat exhaustion and heat stroke, venomous animals (scorpions, spiders, snakes, Gila monsters), oases, sandstorms, and flash floods. The episode closes with a listener mail from Stacy Coombs about the show's conversational style and a sign-off plugging the website and email.

entities.name: The Golden Age of Grave Robbing

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about podcast burnout, Chuck's movie notes for Movie Crush, Point Break, Keanu Reeves, and Ben Sinclair from High Maintenance. They also tease about the desert survival article Chuck wrote, with song-title sidebars.

segments.title: Desert basics and the lack of water
segments.summary: The hosts explain that deserts are defined by lack of available water, not sand. Antarctica is the largest desert. Most desert ground is exposed bedrock and pebbles, and sand covers only a small part. Hot deserts heat up quickly under the sun.

segments.title: Dehydration and water rationing
segments.summary: Symptoms of dehydration are described, including dark urine, dry mouth, sunken eyes, and a faster heartbeat. Vomiting and diarrhea are very bad signs. The advice is to ration sweat, not water, and to drink before feeling thirsty. Experts recommend about a gallon a day.

segments.title: Finding water and moving safely
segments.summary: Advice on finding water: follow trails, watch circling birds and animals, dig where there is wet sand, and take the flat, longer route rather than climbing mountains. Conserve energy, talk less, and breathe through the nose.

segments.title: Fire and signaling for rescue
segments.summary: Fire is useful for warmth, purifying water, and deterring animals, and it serves as a signal. Making yourself visible is key to rescue. Methods include blowing up a gas tank, raising the hood, using cloth on the antenna, spelling SOS or HELP on the ground, and using a mirror. The hosts discuss practicing mirror signaling and whistles and horn honking.

segments.title: Staying with the car and shade
segments.summary: If stranded, stay with the car and leave a note. Sit in the car's shade, not directly on the ground, because the ground can be about thirty degrees hotter than the air above it. Get feet off the ground and keep clothing on to let sweat cool you and block UV.

segments.title: Shoes, cardboard hats, and stuck cars
segments.summary: Remove shoes in shade so feet do not swell. Make a head covering from materials on hand. For a car stuck in sand, let a little air out of the tires, apply steady throttle, and rock the wheels, without letting out too much air.

segments.title: Oases and walking pace
segments.summary: An oasis forms when wind removes enough sand to expose groundwater, and some oases are large enough for towns, such as the Cargo Oasis in the Sahara. Walk slowly and take regular breaks. In groups, set the pace by the slowest person.

segments.title: Heat cramps, exhaustion, and heat stroke
segments.summary: The three stages of heat illness are heat cramps, heat exhaustion, and heat stroke, caused by water and salt imbalance. Cramps are treated with fluids such as sports drinks or water, and rest in shade. Heat exhaustion brings irritability, headache, and nausea. Heat stroke is dangerous: the body's cooling fails, proteins misfold, the heart races, and there can be hallucinations, unconsciousness, or cardiac arrest. Cool the body and get into shade.

segments.title: Venomous animals and bites
segments.summary: Desert dangers include spiders such as brown recluses and black widows, scorpions (some species with dangerous venom), rattlesnakes, and coral snakes. The rhyme 'red touches yellow' describes the coral snake. Gila monsters and Mexican beaded lizards are venomous. For a bite or sting, stay in shade, do not elevate the wound, and apply a cool compress.

segments.title: Sandstorms and flash floods
segments.summary: Sandstorms can last hours or weeks. Pull over, turn on hazards, roll up windows, and cover the face with a wet cloth. Desert ground does not absorb water well, so rain can cause flash floods. More people drown in the desert than die of thirst. Chuck recounts a New Mexico storm.

segments.title: Listener mail from Stacy Coombs
segments.summary: Stacy Coombs writes that the conversational style is a strength, the show is part of her relationship, and her favorite episode is the Golden Age of Grave Robbing. The hosts reply about a live show.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh direct listeners to the website, social links, the email address, and the HowStuffWorks site.
